text: Chapter 20

Scrap wanted to know so much about her mother that Arundel soon had to start making things up. He would talk about anything she wanted just to be near her, see her, and hear her speak. But he actually knew very little about the Droitwich family and their circle—other than meeting them at large literary events and entertaining them at lunch and dinner parties. To them, he was always just
Mister Arundel,
never
Ferdinand.

He only knew the same gossip published in evening papers and discussed in gentlemen's clubs. However, he was good at storytelling. Once he ran out of real facts, he began making things up to answer her questions and keep her with him. It was easy to attribute some of his own funny thoughts to other people and pretend they had done them. Scrap, whose affection for her parents grew stronger during her absence, was desperate for news and listened with growing interest to the stories he spun.

At first, it was just ordinary updates. He had run into her mother here and there; she looked well and said this or that. But soon, the comments he attributed to Lady Droitwich took on a surprising quality: they became hilarious.
Mother said that?
Scrap interrupted, surprised.
And soon, Lady Droitwich was doing funny things as well as saying them.
Mother did that?
Scrap asked, wide-eyed.
Arundel got into his groove. He attributed some of his own best ideas to Lady Droitwich, along with any charming, funny stories he could think of—or make up, since he had a very active imagination.

Scrap's eyes widened with wonder and pride. How funny—imagine her mother doing that! What an absolute darling. Did she really do that? How adorable. And did she really say that? How brilliant of her to think of it. What kind of face did Lloyd George make?

She laughed and laughed, wishing she could hug her mother. Time flew by. It grew dusk, then nearly dark, while Mister Arundel kept entertaining her. It was a quarter to eight before she suddenly remembered dinner.
Oh, my goodness!
she exclaimed, jumping up.
Yes, it is late,
Arundel said.
I'll go ahead quickly and send the maid to show you in. I must run, or I'll never be ready in time—
And she hurried up the path as swiftly as a young, slender deer.

Arundel followed. He didn't want to arrive sweaty, so he walked slowly. Fortunately, he was near the top. Francesca came down the pergola to guide him inside, and after showing him where to wash up, she left him in the empty drawing room to cool off by the crackling wood fire.

He stood in one of the deep window alcoves, as far from the fire as possible, looking at the distant lights of Mezzago. The drawing room door was open, and the house was quiet with the usual pre-dinner hush while everyone was in their rooms dressing. Briggs was in his room, tossing aside one ruined tie after another. Scrap was in her room, hurrying into a black dress with the vague hope that Mister Briggs wouldn't notice her as much in black. Missus Fisher was pinning the lace shawl that transformed her day dress into evening wear, using the brooch Ruskin had given her for her wedding—two pearl lilies tied with a blue enamel ribbon bearing the gold inscription Esto perpetua. Mister Wilkins was sitting on the edge of the bed brushing his wife's hair—showing how much more affectionate he had become in this third week—while Lotty sat in front of him, putting buttons into his clean shirt. Rose, already dressed, sat by her window reflecting on her day.

Rose was fully aware of what had happened to Mister Briggs. Even if she hadn't noticed, Lotty had made it obvious with her frank comments when they sat on the wall after tea. Lotty was thrilled to see more love at San Salvatore, even if it was one-sided. She said that once Rose's husband arrived—now that Missus Fisher had finally softened up (Rose objected to Lotty's phrasing, but Lotty claimed she got the expression from Keats)—there wouldn't be a happier place on earth than San Salvatore.
Your husband might be here very soon,
Lotty said, swinging her legs,

maybe tomorrow evening if he leaves right away. We'll have a wonderful last few days before we go home refreshed. I don't think any of us will ever be the same. And I wouldn't be surprised if Caroline ends up liking young Briggs. It's in the air. You just have to love people here.

Rose sat at her window thinking about this. Lotty was so optimistic... yet her predictions had come true with Mister Wilkins and Missus Fisher. If only it would happen for Frederick too! Rose, who had temporarily stopped thinking about Frederick during her walk, was now thinking about him more than ever.

That brief period of admiration had been funny and delightful, but of course it ended the moment Caroline appeared. Rose knew she couldn't compete. Anyone could see Lady Caroline's unique beauty. Still, being admired and appreciated made a person feel so warm and confident, as if they really deserved it. It seemed to bring hidden parts of her to life. She was sure she had been entertaining and even pretty this afternoon. She was certain of it; she had seen it in Mister Briggs's eyes as clearly as in a mirror. For a short time, she felt like a sluggish fly brought back to life by a warm fire on a cold day. She still felt a pleasant thrill just remembering it. It was fun having an admirer, even briefly. No wonder people liked it; it really did make you feel alive.

Even though it was over, she still felt a glow of excitement and optimism she hadn't felt since she was a girl—much like how Lotty must feel all the time. She dressed carefully. Even though she knew Mister Briggs wouldn't notice her now, she enjoyed seeing how pretty she could make herself look. She almost put a red camellia in her hair by her ear. She held it there for a moment, and it looked incredibly attractive, matching the color of her lips perfectly. But she took it out with a smile and a sigh and placed it in water where flowers belonged. She mustn't be silly, she thought. She had to think of her charity work and the poor. Soon she would be back in London, and how ridiculous would a camellia in her hair look then? Completely absurd.

But she was determined about one thing: the moment she got home, she would have a serious talk with Frederick. If he didn't come to San Salvatore, that would be her very first step. She should have done it long ago, but she had always been held back by how much she loved him and how much she feared getting hurt again. But now, even if he hurt her as much as possible, she would still talk to him. Not that he ever hurt her on purpose; she knew he didn't mean to and often had no idea he had done it. For a writer, Rose thought, Frederick didn't seem to have much empathy or imagination. Anyway, she told herself as she stood up, things couldn't go on like this. She was going to speak up. She was tired of this separate life and cold loneliness. Why shouldn't she be happy? Why on earth shouldn't she be loved and allow herself to love?

She looked at her clock. There were still ten minutes before dinner. Tired of waiting in her room, she decided to go to Missus Fisher's balcony, which would be empty now, and watch the moon rise over the sea.
With that plan, she walked into the empty upper hall, but she was drawn to the drawing room by the warm glow of firelight shining through the open door.

It looked so cheerful. The fire completely changed the room. In the daylight, it was dark and ugly, but now it was transformed, just as she had been by the warmth of... no, she mustn't be silly. She must think of the poor; that thought always brought her back to reality.

She peeped inside. Firelight, flowers, and the dark blue night visible through the narrow windows. How lovely. San Salvatore was such a sweet place. And that beautiful lilac on the table—she wanted to go over and smell it...
But she never reached the lilac. She took one step toward it and froze. Standing in the far corner, looking out the window, was Frederick.
All the blood rushed to Rose's heart, and it felt like it stopped beating.
Frederick had come.
She stood perfectly still. He hadn't heard her and didn't turn around. She just stared at him. The miracle had actually happened; he was here.
She held her breath. He must need her, since he had come immediately. He must have been thinking of her and longing for her too...

Her heart, which had seemed to stop, was now racing so fast it took her breath away. Frederick did love her—he had to, or why would he be here? Perhaps her absence had made him realize he wanted her. Now, the talk she had planned would be so easy.

Her thoughts came to a halt. Her mind went blank. She couldn't think logically; she could only see and feel. She had no idea how it had happened, but it was a miracle. God could perform miracles, and He had performed this one.
Her thoughts trailed off again.
Frederick—
she tried to say, but no sound came, or if it did, the crackling fire drowned it out.
She had to go closer. She began to walk toward him very quietly.
He didn't move. He hadn't heard a thing.
She crept closer and closer, and the crackling fire hid the sound of her steps.
She stopped for a second, unable to breathe. She felt a wave of fear. What if... but no, he had come.
She stepped closer, right up behind him. Her heart was beating so loudly she thought he must hear it. Couldn't he feel her presence? Didn't he know she was there?
Frederick,
she whispered, her voice barely a breath because of her racing heart.
He spun around.
Rose!
he exclaimed, staring at her in shock.
But she didn't notice his stunned look. Her arms were already around his neck and her cheek was pressed against his. She whispered in his ear,
I knew you would come. Deep down, I always knew you would come.
